newsitem.title: UK: POLL - UK output prices seen flat in June.
newsitem.headline: POLL - UK output prices seen flat in June.

text.p: British June producer price data, due to be published on Monday Monday at 0830 GMT, are unlikely to show any build-up of background inflation pressures.
A Reuter poll of economists produced a consensus expecting unchanged output prices in June, leaving them just 1.1 percent higher than a year earlier.
Input prices are forecast to have fallen 0.5 percent on the month and 7.8 percent year-on-year as the pound's strength continues to cut imported raw materials prices.
"Input prices are still being held down by the strength of the exchange rate and that is feeding through to output prices," said David Walton, UK economist at Goldman Sachs.
He agreed with the consensus forecast for output prices. The pound, up more than 20 percent in less than a year, has steadily eroded import prices.
The figures are unlikely to shake British financial markets for two reasons.
Firstly, producer prices have been weak for as long as anybody can remember. The inflationary threat posed to the British economy is coming from frantic high street spending.
Secondly, retail prices for June were released earlier this week. Underlying inflation jumped to 2.7 percent year-on-year from 2.5 in May. Usually, RPI data come out after the PPI.
The Bank of England, concerned by the price pressures that unrestrained consumer spending could create, raised interest rates by a quarter-point to 6.75 percent on Thursday.
Most economists expect more rate rises to come, so it is clear that enduringly weak producer prices do not really enter into the policy equation.
"They are a very small part of the inflation jigsaw," said Adam Cole, UK economist at HSBC James Capel. He forecast unchanged output prices in June but saw them up 1.2 percent from a year ago.
"There are no signs of inflation pressure coming through in manufacturing at all but the problems come in the other three-quarters of the economy, the service sector," Cole said.
There, output is much more buoyant and inflation is threatening from retailers' pricing policies and growing wage pressures.
Cole said producer prices were only important in terms of the extent that retailers pass on the fall in their costs to consumers.

"Generally, it seems they are taking them as a boost to margins and not passing them on," Cole said. "With consumer spending so strong, they are likely to get away with it. We are unlikely to see weak pipeline inflation pressures feeding through to the high street."
